title: Intrinsic Benefits of Categorical Distributional Loss: Uncertainty-aware Regularized Exploration in Reinforcement Learning

strengths: The paper addresses an important question: why learning return distributions can outperform learning expected returns. The fitted-iteration perspective offers a useful framework for comparing objectives and representations.

Applying Sinkhorn matching to return particles is a plausible algorithmic direction. Comparisons with DQN, C51, QR-DQN, and MMD on ten Atari games, together with limited hyperparameter studies, provide preliminary evidence of practical feasibility.

The authors explicitly acknowledge that finite-regularization Sinkhorn losses need not yield contraction and that greedy action selection does not ensure exploration. No material research-ethics concern is apparent in the reported experiments.
weaknesses: The central decomposition in Eq. 4 is invalid for general return distributions. Writing p = (1−ε)δ_E[Z] + εμ with a probability distribution μ requires p to have an atom of mass at least 1−ε at its mean. An absolutely continuous distribution has no such atom; the proposed subtraction produces a signed measure rather than a probability distribution. Taking ε = 1 removes the claimed expectation component. This fundamentally undermines Proposition 2 and the regularization and acceleration interpretations built on it.

The connection to maximum-entropy RL is not established. Theorem 1 introduces a new Bellman operator with a cross-entropy reward adjustment, but minimizing the distribution-fitting loss does not imply this reward adjustment. Appendix D invokes ordinary policy-evaluation convergence for fixed, bounded modified rewards; it does not establish equivalence to standard distributional RL or justify convergence when the reward adjustment changes with θ.

Theorem 4 contradicts the stated Sinkhorn objective. With the specified cost c(x,y) = −|x−y|² and point masses u = δ_0, v = δ_1, Eq. 13 equals −2 for every regularization value, whereas the claimed Wasserstein limit is +2. Thus the stated loss is not a nonnegative distribution discrepancy. This may reflect a sign error, but it changes the optimization objective and leaves the implemented algorithm unclear.

The acceleration result has additional substantive gaps. Theorem 3 specifies ε = 1/(1+τ), while Appendix I uses ε = 1/(1+κ). Part (3) infers nonconvergence from an upper bound, which cannot establish nonconvergence. Moreover, the comparator is likelihood fitting at the mean rather than the least-squares objective of expectation-based RL, and the required small-κ condition is neither derived from distribution-approximation error nor tested experimentally.

The defensible stability analysis is restricted to a softmax linear model with fixed bounded features and a fixed supervised target distribution. It does not establish stability or generalization for the learned neural representations or Sinkhorn objective used experimentally. Under the same fixed-feature assumptions, squared loss is also convex and smooth; its globally unbounded gradient is a separate issue. The valid result largely specializes existing histogram-regression and convex-SGD stability theory, limiting the demonstrated theoretical originality.

The empirical evidence cannot independently support the broad performance claims. Results on ten games have mixed rankings, with no aggregate analysis or comparison against acknowledged stronger methods such as IQN/FQF. Seed counts, the meaning of shaded bands, important Atari evaluation settings, and a concrete code reference are missing. Runtime comparisons are also absent despite the additional particle-transport computation.

The experiments do not test the proposed mechanisms through controlled measurements of gradient variance, generalization, or regularization effects. Figure 2 uses a single-game t-SNE visualization labeled by each agent’s own policy, which cannot establish tighter clusters in the original representation or identify 'correct' action classes. The high-dimensional sample-complexity motivation also does not directly apply to the scalar return distributions studied here.
